(Direct ethnic, religious or sexual-orientation slurs are commonly used in some of these settings but are omitted here; researchers often cite them indirectly as “the N-word,” “the F-word,” etc.)

1. IMMIGRATION  
  • “They don’t belong here.”  
    – Target: Undocumented immigrants, asylum-seekers  
    – Context: Campaign speeches, Facebook/Twitter threads  
    – Function: Exclusionary boundary-drawing (“in” vs. “out”)  
  • “They’re taking our jobs.”  
    – Target: Immigrant labor (legal or not)  
    – Context: Town-hall meetings, right-wing op-eds  
    – Function: Economic scapegoating, stoking fear of unemployment  
  • “Illegal aliens”  
    – Target: Undocumented migrants  
    – Context: Policy debates, mainstream media headlines  
    – Function: Legal-status othering, dehumanization (referring to persons as “aliens”)  
  • “Anchor babies”  
    – Target: U.S.-born children of undocumented parents  
    – Context: Anti-immigration commentaries  
    – Function: Delegitimizing birthright citizenship, coded sexism/racism  
  • “They’re invaders.”  
    – Target: Refugees, migrants from “rest of the world”  
    – Context: Far-right rallies, conspiratorial blogs  
    – Function: Militaristic threat framing  

2. RACE & ETHNICITY  
  • “Welfare queens”  
    – Target: Poor, often Black single mothers  
    – Context: Political ads (1970s–), cable-news punditry  
    – Function: Racialized economic scapegoating (“undeserving poor”)  
  • “Inner-city thugs” or “urban criminals”  
    – Target: Young Black or Latino men  
    – Context: Crime-reporting, crime-policy debates  
    – Function: Criminalization, heightening fear of neighborhoods  
  • “They breed too much.”  
    – Target: Minority women (e.g. in white-supremacist discourse)  
    – Context: Extremist forums, hate-speech podcasts  
    – Function: Dehumanizing/eugenic rhetoric  
  • “They want to replace us.”  
    – Target: Non-white populations  
    – Context: Alt-right manifestos, online message boards  
    – Function: Conspiracy-theory scapegoating (“Great Replacement”)  

3. RELIGION  
  • “Radical Islamic terrorists”  
    – Target: Muslims (equating entire faith with extremists)  
    – Context: Counterterrorism speeches, cable-news panels  
    – Function: Securitization, broad-brush demonization  
  • “Sharia is coming for us.”  
    – Target: Islamic law, Muslim communities  
    – Context: Anti-Sharia rallies, talk-radio call-ins  
    – Function: Moral panic, cultural threat framing  
  • “They’re not loyal to our country.”  
    – Target: Arab- or South Asian-descent Muslims  
    – Context: Congressional debates, campaign ads  
    – Function: Questioning patriotism, loyalty tests  

4. SEXUAL ORIENTATION & GENDER IDENTITY  
  • “Degenerates”  
    – Target: LGBTQ+ persons  
    – Context: Conservative speeches, social-media comment threads  
    – Function: Moral condemnation, framing as societal decay  
  • “Bathroom predators”  
    – Target: Transgender individuals  
    – Context: Legislative hearings on restroom laws  
    – Function: Fear-mongering sexual-safety argument  
  • “The gay agenda”  
    – Target: LGBT activists  
    – Context: Religious-conservative blogs, sermons  
    – Function: Conspiracy framing (“hidden plan” to reshape society)  

5. POLITICAL IDEOLOGY & SOCIOECONOMIC CLASS  
  • “Snowflakes”  
    – Target: College students, liberals/progressives  
    – Context: Twitter memes, late-night-host jabs  
    – Function: Dismissal of political correctness, emotional fragility trope  
  • “Cultural Marxists”  
    – Target: Left-wing academics, sometimes Jews (anti-Semitic code)  
    – Context: Far-right manifestos, conspiracy podcasts  
    – Function: Delegitimizing social-justice movements as secret cabal  
  • “Globalist elites”  
    – Target: International financiers, cosmopolitan politicians (often coded anti-Semitic)  
    – Context: Populist stump speeches, fringe-news sites  
    – Function: Anti-elitist populism, conspiratorial scapegoating  
  • “They’re out of touch.”  
    – Target: Political opponents, “coastal elites”  
    – Context: Campaign ads, local debates  
    – Function: Populist contrast (“everyday people” vs. remote elites)
